paper_title: AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation
core_problem: Building powerful LLM-based applications and agents requires flexible multi-agent conversation with customizable, conversable agents that can combine LLMs, tools, and human inputs, and programmable interaction patterns to enable meaningful task progress across diverse domains.
methodology_summary: AutoGen is an open-source framework for building LLM applications via multiple agents that converse to accomplish tasks. Agents are conversable, customizable and can be based on LLMs, tools, humans or combinations. The framework adopts conversation programming centered on inter-agent conversations, allowing developers to define a set of conversable agents with specific capabilities and roles and flexibly define interaction behaviors using natural language and code. Agents can operate autonomously in multi-turn chats or solicit human inputs, supporting human-in-the-loop and modular combination of LLM capabilities.
datasets_eval: No specific benchmark datasets are named in the provided context; empirical studies are described across example applications in mathematics, coding, question answering, operations research, online decision-making, entertainment, etc.
empirical_results: Empirical studies demonstrate the effectiveness of the framework in many example applications spanning mathematics, coding, question answering, operations research, online decision-making, entertainment, etc. Customizable and conversable agents enable rapid creation of role-specific agents e.g., code writer, code executor, human feedback wiring, output validation with autonomous multi-turn conversation and optional human solicitation. Conversation programming streamlines development of intricate LLM application workflows via defining agents and flexible conversation patterns.
explicit_limitations: ChatGPT was not evaluated on the whole dataset due to substantial manual effort and hourly message-number limitation. Multi-agent debate and LangChain ReAct were not evaluated as they underperformed vanilla GPT-4 on a smaller test set. Developing applications where agents make meaningful progress requires developers to specify and mold multi-agent conversations. Privacy and data protection considerations are noted.
